extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, in-house counsel, patent owners and petitioners involved in PTAB/post-grant proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: A practice-oriented digest summarizing procedural and substantive standards, timelines, and strategic considerations for post‑grant proceedings before the USPTO/PTAB (IPR, PGR, CBM, reexamination, reissue, supplemental exam, derivation, interferences, appeals).

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR permissible grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The only permissible grounds for challenging a patent in an IPR petition are anticipation and obviousness based on prior art patents or printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR challenges are limited to patents and printed publications (product prior art not allowed). IPR is available after the initial 9‑month post‑issuance PGR window closes. Use IPR when invalidity theory fits these grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR institution standard (reasonable likelihood)
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB evaluates the IPR petition and any preliminary response to determine whether the challenger has established a reasonable likelihood that at least one challenged claim is unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reasonable likelihood is met for at least one challenged claim, the PTAB will institute trial as to all grounds in the petition (even if some grounds have deficiencies). Institution decision is typically issued within three months after patent owner preliminary response or when due. If instituted, Board issues a scheduling order to complete the proceeding within the statutory 12‑month deadline (subject to joinders/extensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR timing availability
rubrics_metrics.description: An IPR is only available nine months after a patent has issued (in the nine months directly after patent issuance, a different procedure, post‑grant review, is available).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan timing between PGR/IPR windows; petitions cannot be filed during the initial 9‑month PGR window for post‑AIA patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of proof for invalidating a patent in an IPR proceeding is a 'preponderance of the evidence' (~51%) rather than 'clear and convincing evidence'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lower standard versus district court litigation increases the challenger's likelihood of success; incorporate into forum-selection and settlement strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: If challengers do not prevail, they may be estopped from raising grounds that were raised or could have reasonably been raised in the IPR in subsequent proceedings before the USPTO, federal courts, and the US International Trade Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully consider grounds included in an IPR petition because losing can bar those grounds later; weigh breadth of petition against estoppel risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR availability and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A PGR is available only in the nine months following issuance of a patent that issued from an application filed after March 15, 2013; the scope of challenges is broader than IPR and includes ineligible subject matter, lack of utility, lack of novelty, obviousness, lack of written description or enablement, and double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR can reach almost all invalidity theories (except equity jurisprudence like inequitable conduct). Use PGR to raise 35 U.S.C. §101 and §112 issues that IPR cannot reach, but be mindful of PGR's potentially broader estoppel effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR institution standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure institution of a PGR, a petitioner must either show that it is more likely than not that at least one claim of the challenged patent is unpatentable, or raise a novel or unsettled legal question important to other patents or applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'more likely than not' standard is higher than the IPR reasonable‑likelihood standard; alternatively, emphasize novel legal questions of broader importance to obtain institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR estoppel breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel after a PGR likely applies to estop the petitioner from raising arguments in subsequent litigation or other administrative proceedings that were raised or reasonably could have been raised during the PGR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PGR allows many more grounds than IPR, the potential estoppel is broader; evaluate this when deciding between PGR and other options.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM eligibility and limits (transitional program)
rubrics_metrics.description: CBM review applied only to 'covered business method patents' covering methods/apparatus for data processing or operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service; technological inventions were excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBM required the claims to cover financial‑nature products/services (incidental financial activity likely excluded). CBM petitions were available only to persons accused of infringement and could not be filed if a PGR was available. Note: program sun‑set on Sept. 15, 2020.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM estoppel differences
rubrics_metrics.description: CBM estoppel provisions differed from PGR/IPR: grounds not raised in a prior CBM but that reasonably could have been raised could still be raised in subsequent district court proceedings, but a challenger could not pursue subsequent USPTO actions based on any ground actually raised or reasonably could have been raised in the prior CBM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand differences in preclusion between forums when selecting CBM (historical) versus PGR/IPR strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte reexamination scope and features
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex parte reexamination may be requested to challenge novelty or nonobviousness based on printed publications and patents only; other types of prior art (such as product prior art) cannot be raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests can be filed anytime after grant and up to six years after expiration (case‑by‑case variations possible). Third‑party involvement largely ceases after filing; requests can be anonymous; no estoppel applies to requester; patent owner may amend/add claims during reexam, potentially strengthening patent. USPTO decides if submitted prior art raises a substantial new question of patentability (SNQ). No statutory time limit but USPTO may conduct with 'special dispatch.' Weigh anonymity and no‑estoppel advantage against risk that patent owner can improve the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue requirements and bases
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue application may be filed by a patent owner to correct an error in a patent; reissue is proper where the patent is 'wholly inoperative or partly inoperative or invalid' as a result of the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common bases: claims too narrow or too broad (broadening reissue must be filed within two years of issuance), disclosure inaccuracies, foreign priority errors, incorrect references to co‑pending applications. Use reissue to strengthen patents prior to litigation or correct substantive drafting errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination scope and SNQ standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplemental examination allows a patent owner to have the USPTO consider, reconsider, or correct information relevant to the patent (not limited to patents/printed publications); items can include §101, §102, §103, public use/sale, §112 issues, and double‑patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard to grant supplemental examination is whether one or more presented items raises a substantial new question of patentability (SNQ). USPTO will conduct supplemental examination within three months of a proper request; if SNQ is found, ex parte reexamination will be ordered, and an ex parte reexam certificate will issue when complete. Supplemental examination can be used to mitigate inequitable conduct concerns under 35 U.S.C. §257(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party preissuance submission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Third‑party preissuance submissions permit third parties to submit patents, published patent applications, and other printed publications with a concise description of the asserted relevance of each submitted item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions must be timely: before mailing of notice of allowance and before the later of six months from publication or mailing of a first office action rejecting any claim. Use to oppose competitor applications early; be mindful that submissions can cause examiners to incorporate prior art and narrow claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation petition requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To initiate a derivation proceeding, a petitioner must file its own patent application and a petition within one year of publication of a pending application or one year of issuance of a patent (whichever is earlier) that claims the same or substantially the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition must state with particularity the basis for finding (1) that an individual named in the earlier‑filed application derived the invention from an individual named in the petition, and (2) that the earlier application was filed without authorization. A petition is insufficient unless supported by substantial evidence including at least one affidavit detailing corroborated communications and lack of authorization. PTAB may correct inventor naming, refuse earlier claims, or cancel involved patent claims. Use derivation when inventorship/ownership is disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent interference standing and phases (pre‑AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interferences determine which party was first to invent for claims with effective filing dates before March 16, 2013; only an applicant with a pending application containing allowable claims toward the same or substantially the same invention has standing (examiners can also declare interferences sua sponte).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceeding has two stages: preliminary phase allowing broad validity challenges (limited discovery like expert depositions) and priority phase to establish earliest conception/reduction to practice (includes exchange of confidential invention records). Interference is useful where litigation is the alternative for ownership disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte appeal procedural requirements and waiver
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application has been twice rejected or a final office action issued, a notice of appeal may be filed (within three months of a final office action, or six months with fee), triggering a two‑month deadline to file an appeal brief (extendable up to five months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal brief must articulate all arguments to overcome examiner rejection; arguments not raised may be waived. Examiner's answer may respond; applicant may file a reply brief and request an oral hearing. Use appeal brief to preserve issues for Board review.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB exercise of discretion in view of parallel district court (Fintiv factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Apple v. Fintiv, the PTAB may consider six factors when determining whether to institute an IPR when there is a parallel district court proceeding: (1) whether the court granted a stay or evidence exists that a stay may be granted if instituted; (2) proximity of court’s trial date to PTAB’s projected statutory deadline; (3) investment in parallel proceeding by court and parties; (4) overlap between issues raised in IPR petition and parallel proceeding; (5) whether petitioner and district court defendant are the same party; (6) other circumstances impacting Board’s exercise of discretion, including the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB takes a holistic view evaluating efficiency, fairness, and merits. Since 2018 PTAB has relied on §314(a) to deny institution when parallel proceedings are advanced. Consider these factors in forum/timing strategy and whether to seek stays in district court.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAS all‑claims‑or‑none institution rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Following SAS Institute Inc. v. Iancu, when the PTAB institutes a proceeding it must decide the patentability of all claims originally challenged by the petitioner (the PTAB will institute as to all claims or none).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners should ensure all challenged claims meet institution thresholds because institution now triggers review of every challenged claim. SAS temporarily caused a spike in instituted petitioned claims but institution rates returned to prior levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery rules — routine and additional (Garmin factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine discovery permitted in all proceedings includes exhibits cited in papers or testimony, cross‑examination of testimonial witnesses, and relevant information inconsistent with a party's position. Additional discovery may be available if in the 'interests of justice.' Garmin factors for additional discovery: (1) more than a possibility and mere allegation; (2) litigation positions and underlying basis; (3) ability to generate equivalent information by other means; (4) easily understandable instructions; (5) requests not overly burdensome to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garmin's list is non‑exhaustive. Board has granted additional discovery in some cases (e.g., contracts/communications where highly relevant). Frame discovery requests to satisfy Garmin factors; anticipate limits on scope and burdensomeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burdens of persuasion for motions to amend (USPTO rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under USPTO final rules, a patent owner bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that a motion to amend complies with statutory and regulatory requirements; a petitioner bears the burden of persuasion, by a preponderance of the evidence, that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This codifies post‑Aqua Products practice (petitioner bears unpatentability burden). Board may, 'in the interests of justice,' exercise discretion to grant or deny a motion to amend for reasons supported by readily identifiable and persuasive evidence of record, but such evidence is limited to related‑proceeding evidence or judicially noticeable district court evidence in most cases. Patent owners should prepare motions to amend and supporting evidence accordingly; petitioners should prepare robust opposition evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to amend practice and preliminary guidance (revised MTA timeline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion to amend practice has evolved to include option of filing an initial motion to amend, receiving preliminary guidance from the Board, and then filing a revised motion to amend addressing the Board's preliminary guidance (PO may indicate whether it requests preliminary guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revised MTA timeline alters scheduling if a revised motion to amend (rMTA) is filed: Board adjusts schedule. Use preliminary guidance to refine substitute claims and supporting arguments; be mindful of sequencing and timing (deadlines for oppositions, replies, sur‑replies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board's authority to raise grounds when system failure (Hunting Titan / Lectrosonics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precedential decisions (e.g., Hunting Titan, Lectrosonics) indicate the Board 'may step in if there is a clear failure in that system' and may raise grounds of unpatentability a petitioner has not advanced or has insufficiently developed in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Board discretion is anticipated to be limited and used rarely (e.g., injustice from procedural defects). Parties should be prepared for Board‑initiated grounds in exceptional cases and address record evidence accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time windows and limitations across proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Various proceedings have discrete timing windows and limitations: PGR and IPR availability windows (PGR within 9 months of issuance for post‑AIA patents; IPR available after 9 months); broad limitations for ex parte reexam (up to six years after expiration, case‑by‑case); broadening reissue within two years; third‑party preissuance submission strict windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically choose proceedings in light of these time bars; missing a window can foreclose remedies or forum choices.
